passage: The canteen queue was long and the bell was about to ring. Nitin leaned over Varun's shoulder and grabbed the marks slip from his hand. "Twelve out of thirty! Ha, Varun the genius!" A few kids in the queue turned. Varun's cheeks burned and his stomach dropped. For a second he wanted to snatch it back, or shout something worse. Then he took a breath. "Yeah, I need to practise that chapter," he said, reaching for the slip. "One test isn't all of me." Nitin blinked; he'd expected a fight. Varun moved up in the queue. He remembered Nitin's dictation notebook, with red pen all over it, and said nothing more.

qa.q: What did Nitin grab from Varun's hand in the queue?
What was Varun feeling when his cheeks burned and his stomach dropped?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, and briefly tempted to snatch back the slip or shout something worse.

qa.q: What choice helped Varun handle Nitin's laughing, and why?
qa.a: Taking a breath and answering calmly, then moving up in the queue, worked because it gave Nitin no fight and kept Varun's dignity.

qa.q: How might Nitin have seen Varun's calm reply?
qa.a: He blinked in surprise, since he had expected a fight, and may not have known what to say.

grounding: A child laughed at over his marks feels hurt, answers calmly and remembers the mocker has weak spots too, under time pressure.

passage: Kashish, that boy laughed at your marks? Come, sit on the swing with your Mridul Dadu. When I was your age, I got four out of twenty-five in a geography test. Bhola, the loudest boy in class, grabbed my paper and waved it. "Four! Even my buffalo would get five!" Everyone laughed. My ears burned. I wanted to hit him. Instead I said, "Maybe your buffalo should sit the next test," took my paper back and walked off. Some boys laughed at him then. Later that year I found Bhola crying behind the school because he couldn't read the long words in the Hindi book. I could. So I helped him, and he helped me with maps. You see, beta, one score is just one day. And the one who laughs has weak spots too.

qa.q: What did Bhola say his buffalo would get?
How did young Mridul feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated and angry; his ears burned and he wanted to hit Bhola.

qa.q: What choice in Dadu's story worked better than hitting Bhola?
qa.a: Answering calmly with a joke, taking the paper back and walking away.

qa.q: What was Bhola hiding behind his loud laughing?
qa.a: His own struggle with reading, which he cried about behind the school.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a classmate mocking his low marks, answering calmly and later seeing that the mocker had weak spots too.

passage:
The half-yearly results were pinned on the noticeboard, and the whole of Class 6 crowded round it before the last bus. Joseph found his name: Maths, 28 out of 80. Red ink.
"Twenty-eight!" Pankaj crowed, loud enough for everyone. "Joseph, did you write with your eyes shut?"
A few kids snorted. Joseph's stomach dropped and his face went hot. The bus horn honked outside; he had maybe one minute.
He thought of a hundred nasty replies. Pankaj couldn't swim a single length in PE; everyone knew. But he didn't say it.
"One test, Pankaj," he said evenly. "I'll do better next time." Then he picked up his bag and walked out to the bus.
On the ride home his heart slowed. Pankaj's words had hurt, but they hadn't changed who he was.

qa.q: What did Joseph score in maths?
How did Joseph feel when Pankaj crowed?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed; his stomach dropped and his face went hot.

qa.q: What did Joseph choose instead of a nasty reply?
qa.a: He answered calmly that it was one test and walked out to the bus.

qa.q: What would change if Joseph had mentioned Pankaj's swimming?
qa.a: It could have turned into a public fight and hurt Pankaj too, instead of ending the mockery.

grounding: A boy mocked for his marks answers calmly and walks away, knowing one score does not define him and that the mocker has weak spots too.
